Erik M

📌 [...] Opposable is computer use, but for your phone. You install an Android app, paste one line into Claude Code or Codex, and your agent can open apps, read what's on the screen, tap, type and swipe on a real phone. So it can finally do the stuff that only exists as an app: check a delivery, book something, reply to a message, or grab the 2FA code that always shows up halfway through. You can also just hand a task to the phone itself. Simple things like alarms, texts and settings run without any model, and for the rest there's a small model running on the phone, so it keeps going after you close the laptop. The iPhone part is a bit of a hack. Apple doesn't let any app control other apps, so we use a tiny ESP32 USB stick (about $8) that the iPhone thinks is a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse. You [...] the iPhone thinks is a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse. You flash it from the browser, plug it into your computer, and the agent taps around through AssistiveTouch. It's beta and I'd love for people to try to break it. Payments always wait for you to approve them on the phone, and there's a log of everything the agent did. The Android app is free. If it gets stuck somewhere, I'd really like to hear about it.

It enables seamless task execution — from placing calls and sending texts to managing apps and responding intelligently in real time. Unlike basic assistants, this AI can learn usage patterns and optimize interactions like a true digital agent. Security and privacy are still concerns, but with proper safeguards, the benefits outweigh the risks. Overall, it's a bold step toward more intuitive and hands-free mobile experiences.
